name: Present Perfect (førnutid med "har/er")
explanation: Use present perfect — "har" or "er" + past participle — to ask or talk about whether something has happened, without saying exactly when. This is the natural tense for recommending or discussing entertainment: "Har du set...?" (Have you seen...?) and "Har du hørt...?" (Have you heard...?) both use this pattern. Most verbs take "har"; a small group of movement/change verbs take "er" instead.

examples.danish: Har du set den nye serie på DR?
examples.english: Have you seen the new series on DR?

examples.danish: Jeg har hørt det album flere gange.
examples.english: I have listened to that album several times.

name: Predicative vs. attributive use
explanation: An adjective changes form depending on where it sits in the sentence. Attributive (before the noun): with a common-gender noun (en-word) the adjective stays in its base form (en kedelig film); with a neuter noun (et-word) it takes a -t ending (et kedeligt afsnit). Predicative (after "er"/"var"): it agrees with the subject the same way — base form for a common-gender subject (Filmen var kedelig), -t ending when the subject is neuter or the impersonal "det" (Det var kedeligt at se). Note that adjectives already ending in -ende, like spændende and rørende, never change form in either position. Opinion adjectives about entertainment show up constantly in both positions, so getting the agreement right matters for natural-sounding reviews and recommendations.

examples.danish: Det var kedeligt at se hele sæsonen på én aften.
examples.english: It was boring to watch the whole season in one evening.

examples.danish: Filmen var faktisk slet ikke kedelig.
examples.english: The film was actually not boring at all.
